International advertising: strategy, benefits and best practices

September 19, 2024
Globalisation | Adventures in Globalisation & Localisation | International Development

Some brands seem to be everywhere, in every market and every language. Behind that presence sits a plan: which countries to enter, which channels to buy and how much of the message to change on the way.

If you are weighing up international advertising for your own business, you need answers to three questions. What does it involve, what do you gain and how do you run campaigns that work in more than one market? The sections below cover each.

What is international advertising?

International advertising is the promotion of a product or service in more than one country or region. It goes well beyond translating existing marketing materials, because each market has its own language, culture, regulations, media habits and buying behaviour.

A long-running debate in marketing asks whether you should standardise your message worldwide or adapt it locally. The economist Theodore Levitt argued in a 1983 Harvard Business Review article, “The Globalization of Markets”, that technology was creating global consumers who would accept standardised products. Many researchers have since argued that advertising is tied to culture and has to adapt. In practice, most successful brands keep a consistent global idea and localise the execution.

What are the benefits of international advertising?

Access to new markets

The most obvious benefit is reach. Instead of limiting yourself to one market, you can introduce your products to customers in many countries.

Digital platforms make this easier, because search, social and video advertising let you target specific regions and languages, so your budget goes to the people most likely to respond.

Increased brand awareness

Advertising in several countries builds recognition beyond your home market. When people see your brand repeatedly in their own language, it becomes familiar and easier to trust.

That familiarity can open doors to distributors, retailers and partners that you would not reach from a single market.

Diversified revenue streams

Relying on one market is risky, especially if it faces an economic downturn or new competition. Selling in several countries spreads that risk and gives you more than one source of growth.

How do you build an international advertising strategy?

A good international advertising strategy starts with choosing where to compete, not with choosing channels. Work through these steps in order.

Choose and size your markets

Look at demand, competition, regulation and logistics for each country before you commit budget. UK exporters can get practical advice from the Department for Business and Trade’s Export Support Service.

Set goals for each market

Awareness, leads and sales need different campaigns and different measures. Set a goal and a target for each country, because a mature market and a new one rarely share the same objective.

Decide what to standardise and what to adapt

Keep your brand idea, values and visual identity consistent. Adapt anything that depends on language or culture, such as headlines, humour, imagery, offers, pricing and calls to action.

Plan channels for each market

Media habits differ. Search and social may carry the budget in one country, while video, print or television matter more in another, so research where your audience spends its time.

How does international paid media work across languages?

International paid media means buying advertising space in several countries, usually across search, social, display and video. Two settings matter most: where your ads appear and which languages they use.

Google Ads, for example, treats location and language as separate settings. Location targeting chooses the geographic areas where your ads can appear, while language targeting reaches people based on the language they use, and it does not translate your ad copy for you. A campaign aimed at English speakers in Spain behaves differently from one aimed at Spanish speakers in Spain, so plan campaigns around country and language together.

Do not translate your keywords word for word. People search differently in each language, so keyword research needs to be done natively. Send clicks to a landing page in the same language as the ad, ideally on a properly localised translated website, or you will pay for visitors who leave straight away.

Should you also consider an international TV advertising partner?

It depends on your audience, your goal and your budget. Television still gives broad reach and credibility in many markets, and connected TV lets you target more precisely, but production and airtime are expensive and the rules differ by country.

Consider a local media partner if you need mass awareness, if your product suits a broad audience or if your competitors already advertise on TV in that market. Look for a partner with local audience data, knowledge of regional regulations and experience placing ads in your sector. If your audience is small and specific, digital channels usually let you test and measure with less risk.

Which advertising rules apply abroad?

Each country applies its own laws and advertising codes, so an ad that is legal in the UK may need changes elsewhere. Claims, comparisons, children’s advertising, influencer disclosure and data use are common areas of difference.

The International Chamber of Commerce publishes the ICC Advertising and Marketing Communications Code, a global self-regulatory standard. Its 11th edition, released in September 2024, added guidance on AI and algorithms, influencer marketing and environmental claims. Check the local rules for each market and have a local legal adviser review sensitive campaigns.

What are the best practices for international advertising?

Research your target markets

Study the cultural, economic and social factors that shape buying behaviour. Understanding what people value, how they shop and which platforms they use gives your message a better chance of landing.

Adapt your message

Translating your ads is not enough. What appeals at home may fall flat or offend elsewhere, so adapt and localise visuals, taglines and sometimes the whole concept to the local context. This creative adaptation is often called transcreation.

Work with local partners

Local agencies, media buyers and linguists know the culture, the legal requirements and the consumer preferences. Their insight prevents expensive mistakes and helps your campaign feel native.

Keep a consistent brand voice

Adjust tone and wording for each audience, but keep your core values and personality the same. A recognisable brand builds trust across borders.

Measure and refine

Digital platforms let you track performance by country and language in near real time. Compare results, pause what does not work and move budget to the markets and messages that perform.

How translation supports international advertising

Translation and localisation sit at the centre of every multilingual campaign. A native-speaking linguist checks that your headline means what you intend, that your humour works and that your offer reads naturally, before you spend on media.

BeTranslated helps UK businesses adapt marketing and advertising content for new markets, from ad copy and landing pages to video subtitles and multilingual SEO. Every project is quoted individually, so tell us your markets and languages and we will send a clear quote.

Frequently asked questions

What is international advertising?

International advertising promotes your products or services in more than one country, adapting language, culture, channels and legal claims to each market. It sits within a wider international marketing strategy.

Should I use the same ad in every country?

Rarely. Keep your brand idea and identity consistent, but adapt language, imagery, offers and references to each market, and test local versions before you scale spend.

How do I run paid media campaigns in several languages?

Plan campaigns by country and language, research keywords natively and write or transcreate ad copy for each audience. Send each campaign to a landing page in the matching language.

Do I need a TV advertising partner abroad?

Only if mass reach is your goal and the market supports it. A local partner brings audience data and regulatory knowledge, while digital channels often suit smaller or more specific audiences.

How does translation fit into international advertising?

Translation and localisation make sure your message is accurate and persuasive in each language. A native linguist reviews copy, taglines and landing pages before launch, which reduces the risk of costly mistakes.
